                  ANSWER TO COMMENTS OF THE INDEPENDENT
               MARKET MONITOR FOR PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C.

        Pursuant to Rule 213 of Rules of Practice and Procedure the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), 1 the above-captioned entities (“Applicants”) hereby

answer the Comments of the Independent Market Monitor (“IMM”) 2 for PJM Interconnection,

L.L.C. (“PJM”) filed on May 26, 2026, in the above-captioned docket. Applicants also provide a

public and confidential version of the Supplemental Affidavit of Julie R. Solomon and Jeffrey J.

Opgrand (the “Supplemental Affidavit”), where Ms. Solomon and Dr. Opgrand find the “market

power analysis” accompanying the IMM Report does not “present[] any compelling evidence of an

increase in market power as a result of the [Transaction], particularly in the context of the

to concerns that are unsupported . . . .” 4

          The IMM does not dispute Applicants’ analysis and conclusion that the Transaction clearly

passes the Commission’s competitive screens. 5 Instead, the IMM advocates for the use of pivotal

supplier tests that the Commission has repeatedly rejected and demands that the Commission make

market power determinations based on hypothetical analyses that rely upon opaque data and

economically unsound claims.          Specifically, there is no appropriate basis for the IMM’s

speculative concerns regarding actions by a generation owner with resources on both sides of a

constraint because (i) FERC market rules already prohibit the conduct that the IMM hypothesizes,

(ii) as a result of the Transaction, ArcLight Capital Partners, LLC (“ArcLight Capital”) would have

less of an economic incentive to pursue this hypothetical conduct; and (iii) pursuant to the

Transaction, ArcLight Capital will not obtain the governance rights over day-to-day operations

(including offer submission and dispatch instructions) necessary to engage in the uneconomic

behavior that this hypothetical conduct would require. The IMM also raises concerns regarding

possible future long-term commitments to serve new load, which are not relevant to the

Commission’s review of the Transaction. The Commission should, as it has done before, reject

the IMM’s proposed analytical frameworks, decline to impose the behavioral commitments

requested by the IMM, and authorize the Transaction as consistent with the public interest.

 I.       ANSWER

         A.      The Transaction is Consistent with the Public Interest

         The Application properly showed, and the IMM agrees, that the Transaction “passes the

thresholds defined for the Commission’s initial screen for market power” in all relevant markets. 6

Applicants’ Delivered Price Test (“DPT”) demonstrated that PJM and the AP South, PJM West, 7

and 5004/5005 8 submarkets are generally unconcentrated, 9 both before and after the Transaction,

during all season/load periods, under both the Economic Capacity and Available Economic

Capacity measures. 10 Applicants’ further showed that the Transaction readily passes the relevant

competitive screens in all periods and load conditions, with Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (“HHI”)

changes ranging between 8 and 28 points in the PJM market, 2 and 58 points in the 5004/5005

submarket, 8 and 56 points in the AP South submarket, and 5 and 17 points in the PJM West

submarket. 11     Applicants also properly concluded that the Transaction does not raise any

competitive concerns in PJM’s capacity market, where HHI changes will be 13 points RTO-wide,

based on Installed Capacity, and 32 points in the Mid-Atlantic Area Council Local Deliverability

Area, based on Unforced Capacity. 12 Therefore, Applicants made the necessary showing that the

in PJM—Chesapeake—that is defined by four binding constraints. We note that three of those constraints
also define PJM West and therefore were already included in Applicants’ market power analysis.

 Transaction is consistent with the public interest and does not have an adverse effect on

competition.

        The IMM’s assertion that Applicants must identify offsetting public benefits is incorrect. 13

Section 203 of the FPA does not require Applicants to demonstrate affirmative customer benefits

where, as here, the record shows no adverse effect on competition, rates, or regulation and no

cross-subsidization concern.        The Commission’s public interest review asks whether the

transaction has adverse effects on competition, rates, regulation, and cross-subsidization—not

whether the applicant can identify independent transaction benefits. The only support the IMM

cites to is for an opposition hypothetical, whereby a proposed transaction with some identified

harm to the public could nevertheless be approved if, on balance, the combination of that harm

and identified transaction benefits provided for overall greater public good. 14                 The IMM’s

“balancing” theory, therefore, has no role unless the record first establishes a transaction-specific

adverse effect that must be offset. Here, the IMM has identified no HHI screen failure, no error in

Applicants’ DPT, no adverse effect on rates or regulation, and no cross-subsidization concern.

        B.       The IMM’s Analysis Improperly Relies on Pivotal Supplier Tests

        The IMM’s argument that the Transaction would increase market power 15 relies primarily

on the Three Pivotal Supplier (“TPS”) test as a “key measure of market structure and structural

market power,” 16 even though the Commission has repeatedly rejected the IMM’s use of the TPS



13
     IMM Comments at 3.
14
    The IMM cites solely to FERC’s Merger Policy Statement that recognized the possibility of “unusual
circumstances” where a balancing test may be needed to compel approval of a proposed transaction. IMM
Comments at 3 n.6. The IMM then claims that the Transaction “cannot be approved, including on balance,
without a finding that benefits to the public interest offset the harm identified in the record,” citing solely
to 16 U.S.C. § 824b(b), which does not pertain to the “balancing test.” Id. at 3-4 n. 7.
15

and Dr. Opgrand explain in their Supplemental Affidavit, when the IMM’s analysis considers the

relevant Commission-recognized markets or submarkets and uses the competitive screens required

under FERC’s regulations and precedent, the IMM’s own analysis is consistent with the analysis

set forth in the Application and shows that the Transaction results in minimal HHI changes 18 in

unconcentrated markets and, therefore, does not raise market power concerns.

         The IMM’s related request that the Commission consider broader trends in generation

ownership consolidation in PJM and “aggregate market pivotal suppliers” 19 does not identify a

existing PJM affiliations, including pending transactions treated conservatively as if

consummated.        Any future acquisitions by ArcLight Capital’s affiliates or other market

 FPA does not authorize the Commission to deny a transaction that passes the Commission’s

competitive screens based on generalized concerns about market-wide ownership trends,

speculation about future transactions, or alleged market-wide PJM capacity market conditions that

are not caused by the Transaction. 20

         The IMM also contends that the Merger Policy Statement 21 and Order No. 642 22 require

the Commission to re-evaluate the IMM’s alternative methodology and TPS test results each time

the IMM challenges a proposed transaction, even when a transaction clearly passes the horizontal

Competitive Supplier Screen and notwithstanding prior repeated rejection of the TPS

methodology. 23 The IMM misstates the Commission’s precedent on this matter.

         The Commission adopted the Competitive Analysis Screen as part of Appendix A to the

Merger Policy Statement, and Order No. 642 later codified the Competitive Analysis Screen in

FERC’s regulations. 24      Since inception, the purpose of the screen has been to allow the

Commission to “identify proposed mergers that clearly will not harm competition.” 25 The

Commission adopted the HHI statistic as the screen, because it “is not a perfect or conclusive

measure of a merger’s competitive effect,” 26 but is “conservative enough so that parties and the

Order No. 592, 61 Fed. Reg. 68,595 (Dec. 30, 1996), order on reconsideration, Order No. 592-A, 62 Fed.

 Commission can be confident that an application that clears the screen would have no adverse

effect on competition.” 27 As a result, applicants who demonstrate that their transaction passes the

Competitive Analysis Screen “establish a presumption that the merger raises no market power

concerns.” 28 As the Commission explained in Order No. 642, if the transaction passes the

Competitive Analysis Screen, “the horizontal analysis stops there.” 29 Intervenors may rebut that

presumption by making a “convincing case that the merger has anticompetitive effects despite

passing the screen.” 30 However, that entails challenging the data used by applicants or how they

conducted the analysis, 31 not challenging the Competitive Analysis Screen framework that the

Commission has used for almost 30 years.

           When the Competitive Analysis Screen for a proposed transaction identifies potential

concerns, the Commission will rely on additional analyses and metrics to assess the competitive

effects of the transaction, which may include a pivotal analysis. 32 But when the Competitive

Analysis Screen does not raise any potential concern—as is the case for Applicants’ Transaction—

it is not appropriate for the Commission to consider alternative methodologies or to re-evaluate

alternative methodologies that were previously rejected. 33 Doing so would frustrate the Merger

 Policy Statement’s express goal of providing market participants “greater regulatory certainty and

methodologies in this proceeding as it has done repeatedly before.

        C.        The Chesapeake Submarket is not a Relevant Submarket for the Transaction

        The IMM contends that the Commission should analyze the competitive effects of the

Transaction in a potential new submarket, “Chesapeake.” 35 According to the IMM, Chesapeake

is defined by four frequently binding constraints (Bedington-Black Oak, Conastone-Northwest,

Graceton-Manor, and Nottingham) and includes the DOM, BGE, and PEPCO transmission zones,

but also extends into transmission zones in Pennsylvania and Delaware. 36

        The Commission does not need to determine whether Chesapeake should be studied as a

separate submarket, because it is not a relevant market for the Transaction. 37              The IMM

acknowledges that “[t]here is no overlap of generation between Applicants inside the submarket”38

and that none of the generation facilities covered by the Transaction is located inside



analyses that deviate from the Commission’s longstanding merger review policy framework are not useful
for that effort, particularly where the Commission has repeatedly declined to adopt those alternative
analyses.”).

    Even if Chesapeake was a relevant submarket, Ms. Solomon and Dr. Opgrand note that the “standard
‘2ab’ calculation for the IMM’s ‘Chesapeake’ submarket would be zero.” Supplemental Affidavit at 3. We
note that the IMM did not submit the underlying data and calculations necessary for parties and the
Commission to independently validate the IMM’s request to treat Chesapeake as a separate submarket.
Nevertheless, whether Chesapeake should be treated as a submarket is a moot issue in this case because no
generation facility covered by the Transaction is located inside the claimed Chesapeake submarket and
therefore Chesapeake is not a relevant market under the Commission’s Part 33 regulations. However, if
Chesapeake was a relevant market, it would be critical for parties and the Commission to be able to
promptly and fully access and review such data.
38

 Chesapeake. 39 The Commission’s regulations do not require a horizontal Competitive Analysis

Screen if the parties to the proposed transaction do not have overlapping generation in the same

market. 40 The Commission recently declined to determine whether the ATSI transmission zone

should be considered a submarket because the merging entities no longer had overlapping

generation in ATSI. 41 For the same reason, the Commission should decline to address whether

Chesapeake should be treated as a submarket for the Transaction—there is no overlap of

Applicants’ generation in Chesapeake.

        D.      The Commission Should Reject the IMM’s Arguments Regarding Local
                Market Power on Both Sides of a Constraint

        The IMM argues that the acquisition of generation assets on the low side of a frequently

binding constraint “create[s] structural market power” 42 because the new owner could produce

excess generation for the purpose of increasing congestion and raising prices on the high side of

the constraint for the benefit of affiliated resources located there. 43 The concern is unsupported

by the economic reality, is speculative for multiple reasons, and should be dismissed as not relevant

here.


39

submarket”).

“[a]ffirmatively demonstrates that the merging entities do not currently conduct business in the same
geographic market or that the extent of the business transactions in the same geographic market is de
minimis.”).
41
    See Energy Harbor Corp., 186 FERC ¶ 61,129 at P 122 (2024) (“Eliminating the generation overlap in
the ATSI transmission zone removes the need to conduct a market power analysis for that zone, such that

within PJM.”) (Citations omitted).
42
     IMM Comments at 6.
43
   Id. (“The assets outside the submarket could be used to produce excess energy that causes the
constraints defining the submarket to bind more frequently or at a higher cost, raising prices above
competitive levels inside the submarket to the benefit of current ArcLight generation inside the submarket.
The excess energy could result from a range of behaviors including self scheduling, not following PJM’s
economic dispatch signal, or by submitting inflexible operating parameters.”).

                                                    9
            First, the conduct described by the IMM is illegal and is prohibited by the Commission’s

rules. If the production of excess generation is the result of “not following PJM’s economic

dispatch,” 44 the conduct violates the Market Behavior Rules that require a market-based rate seller

in an organized market to “operate and schedule generating facilities . . . in a manner that complies

with the Commission-approved rules and regulations of the applicable market.” 45 Furthermore,

deliberately producing excess generation from a facility on the low side of the constraint for the

purpose of causing or increasing congestion, and therefore increasing prices for the benefit of

affiliated resources located on the high side of the constraint, is an example of market manipulation

prohibited under the Commission’s rules. 46

           The fact that the conduct described by the IMM is illegal makes the IMM’s concerns purely

speculative. Market participants would have no incentive to engage in illegal behavior that the

IMM and the Office of Enforcement and Regulatory Accounting’s Division of Analytics and

Surveillance could easily detect as part of their market surveillance and that could expose those

executing the strategy to severe monetary sanctions. 47 The IMM does not explain why existing

Commission rules would be inadequate to address such intentional misconduct, nor does it identify

any Transaction-specific basis to presume that Applicants would engage in it. 48

(“The Commission also has found fraud where entities engage in cross-market manipulation schemes,
which involve trading in one market with the intent to move prices in a particular direction to benefit
positions in a related market.”) (Citations omitted).

    See, e.g., American Efficient, LLC, 195 FERC ¶ 61,043 (2026) (imposing monetary sanctions in excess
of $1 billion).

to condition this Transaction under section 203 of the FPA. See infra Section I.F.

         Second, the strategy can be executed only by controlling day-to-day operations of the

generation facilities, including offer submission and dispatch, but ArcLight Capital will not obtain

such control as a result of the Transaction. Pursuant to the Transaction, ArcLight Capital’s affiliate

will acquire a 50 percent interest in Invenergy AMPCI Thermal Power LLC (“IA Thermal

Power”), the indirect owner of the PJM generation resources covered by the Transaction.

Invenergy Clean Power LLC (“ICP”)—which is controlled by Invenergy and not affiliated with

ArcLight Capital—owns the remaining 50 percent interest in IA Thermal Power and serves as the

Asset Manager and the Energy Manager for IA Thermal Power’s resources. As the Asset Manager

and the Energy Manager, ICP manages all commercial, market-facing functions of the PJM

resources 49 and is responsible for the submission of energy offers and the response to dispatch

instructions. Therefore, neither ArcLight Capital nor its affiliates will have the day-to-day control

over offer submission and dispatch that would be necessary to execute the strategy described by

the IMM.

        Third, as Ms. Solomon and Dr. Opgrand explain in the Supplemental affidavit, the strategy

would be uneconomic for ArcLight Capital.               ArcLight Capital is currently affiliated with

substantially more generation on the low side of the constraint than on the high side. Pursuant to

the Transaction, ArcLight Capital’s affiliate will only acquire interests in generation facilities

located on the low side of the constraint. The over-production of energy on the low side posited

by the IMM would be expected to result in lower prices on the low side of the constraint. The

acquisition of additional resources on the low side through the Transaction would increase

ArcLight Capital’s affiliates exposure to the lower prices resulting from the strategy. Therefore,



49
    See Application at 10. The Transaction will not affect ICP’s role as Asset Manager and will not result
in any affiliation between ICP and ArcLight Capital.

                                                   11
 “ArcLight would have less of an incentive to engage in the IMM’s purported uneconomic

overproduction on the low-price side of the Chesapeake constraints.” 50 Furthermore, the IMM’s

concern with a hypothetical strategy fails to account for other factors that would significantly affect

the incentives to engage in the strategy. For instance, affiliates of ArcLight Capital recently

announced a 10-year power supply agreement with Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative

(“SMECO”) backed by a portion of Keys Energy Center, which would be inside the footprint of

Chesapeake, if Chesapeake was treated as a submarket. 51 The agreement, which is structured as a

financial swap, provides that SMECO would receive the benefit of PJM’s settlement prices as the

“floating price,” thus eliminating any incentive for ArcLight Capital’s affiliates to affect the energy

revenues that PJM would pay for that portion of the output of the Keys Energy Center.

         Finally, the strategy described by the IMM cannot be used as a metric or test to analyze the

competitive effects of a proposed transaction under section 203 of the FPA. It is unrelated to, and

independent of, market concentration, market shares, or any reasonable threshold. If concerns

about market abuse through the execution of this strategy were to be a test for the competitive

effects of a proposed transaction, ownership of a single generation resource on one side of any

constraint would arguably preclude the acquisition of any other resource on the other side of the

constraint. 52   This outcome would be nonsensical, divorced from economic theory, and

inconsistent with how the Commission has reviewed horizontal market power in section 203

 proceedings, with cascading effects on every transaction involving generation in neighboring

markets or submarkets.

        In sum, the IMM’s arguments that the Transaction would affect local market power on both

sides of the constraint are purely speculative. No affiliate of ArcLight Capital would have the

ability to engage in this conduct (because it is illegal and ICP will retain the authority to submit

offers and respond to dispatch for the generation covered by the Transaction) or the incentives

(because ArcLight Capital’s affiliates will have substantially more generation on the low side of

the constraint and some of the resources on the high side of the constraint have contractual

arrangements that would negate the benefit of the conduct). Therefore, the Commission should

reject the IMM’s arguments regarding local market power on both sides of the constraint. 53

        E.      The Commission Should Reject the Request for Commitments about the
                “Removal” of Existing Generation to Serve Data Center Load

        The IMM requests a commitment that Applicants “will not remove the Project Companies’

assets from the PJM Capacity Market to serve data center load,” 54 even though nothing in the filing

indicates any intention to enter bilateral power sales agreements to support data center load. The

IMM seems to equate a generation facility’s contractual commitments to serve data center load

with the deactivation and retirement of such generation 55 and fails to explain how a long-term

agreement to serve data center load would be have a different effect on the market than a long-

term agreement with a load serving entity to serve its native load (which could include that load-

serving entity’s data center customers) or conceivably be considered “withholding” capacity from

54

55

                                                13
 the market when power is sold to load in the market. Furthermore, these issues are well outside

the scope of the Commission’s public interest review and should be disregarded as such.

           The IMM’s references to comments filed by the PJM Power Providers Group (“P3”) and

to the investment in Takanock by affiliates of ArcLight Capital and DigitalBridge do not establish

any Transaction-specific adverse effect on competition. 56       Neither P3’s general comments

regarding co-located load nor an investment in a data center power services provider is part of the

Transaction before the Commission. Applicants are not seeking authorization in this docket to

delist or remove any Project Company resource from any PJM market or implement any co-located

load arrangement. The Commission should not impose perceived prophylactic restrictions in this

proceeding based on speculation about potential future arrangements that are not before the

Commission.

           The Commission has previously rejected the IMM’s request for a commitment to keep

existing capacity in the PJM capacity market, noting that the IMM “has not supported the need for

its request with analysis of the impact on competition of any such withdrawal from the PJM

capacity market.” 57 Moreover, the Commission noted that the rates, terms, and conditions of

service applicable to interconnection customers serving co-located load are governed by any

revisions and changes to the PJM tariff resulting from the proceeding in Docket No. EL25-49-

000. 58 And to the extent the IMM wishes to raise broad policy concerns about the industry-wide

issues presented by data center load growth and whether the Commission’s existing policies are

consistent with the policy goals of the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge and the Principles

        The Commission routinely rejects arguments raised in Section 203 proceedings that are

outside the scope of the Commission’s public interest review and should do so here. 61 The

Commission has denied consideration of “issues that are not related to our analysis under FPA

section 203” because such issues “can be resolved in another, more appropriate forum.” 62 This

proceeding is not the appropriate forum for the IMM’s structural claims about the application of

PJM rules to generators serving data center loads. The Commission should therefore disregard the

IMM Comments and requested relief as it has consistently done in similar proceedings, including

in response to similar IMM concerns on the use of existing generation to serve data centers. 63

    A variety of avenues exist for the IMM to raise structural concerns about the use of existing generation
to serve data centers and to seek structural, market-wide remedies. For example, the IMM can lodge
complaints through the PJM stakeholder processes, including any IMM oversight opportunities within the
PJM rules. The IMM could also file a complaint to FERC under Section 206 of the FPA regarding the PJM
market rules. Furthermore, the IMM can address these concerns in any of the many FERC large load
proceedings currently pending.

62
   NRG Energy Inc., 141 FERC ¶ 61,207 at P 89 & n.146 (2012), citing Great Plains Energy Inc., 121
FERC ¶ 61,069 at 50 (2007) (explaining that the Commission will not condition FPA Section 203 approval
on matters that should be addressed in another proceeding or forum); Northeast Generation Co., 117 FERC
¶ 61,068 at P 17 (2006) (explaining that the consideration of environmental concerns are best suited to the
docket addressing the shoreline management plan in question); Boston Edison, 117 FERC ¶ 61,083 at P 44

        The IMM requests the imposition of certain behavioral commitments as a condition for the

        The conditions proposed by the IMM are unrelated to the facts and circumstances of the

Transaction 68 and instead would address what the IMM perceives to be flaws in market power

mitigation provisions of the PJM tariff. The Commission has consistently and properly found that

        Imposing the kind of conditions that the IMM requests exclusively on Applicant and its

affiliates would be undue discrimination and be prohibited under sections 205 and 206 of the

II.       REQUEST FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure does not prohibit

answers to pleadings styled as “comments.” 75 The Commission should not treat the IMM

submission as a protest under Rule 211, because the IMM styled its filing as “comments”.

          If the Commission treats the IMM Comments as a “protest,” Applicants respectfully seek

leave to answer. 76 The Commission has generally permitted answers where, as here, the answer

clarifies issues in dispute, provides information to assist the Commission’s decision-making

          Pursuant to sections 33.8 and 388.112 of the Commission’s regulations, 78 Applicants

request privileged and confidential treatment for portions of the Supplemental Affidavit, which

LLC, 165 FERC ¶ 61,226 at P 37 (2018) (same); Dynegy Inc. 163 FERC ¶ 61,013 at P 15 (2018) (same);
Entergy Nuclear FitzPatrick, LLC, 157 FERC ¶ 61,183 at P 15 (2016) (same); Carolina Power & Light
Co., 97 FERC ¶ 61,048, at 61,278 (2001) (finding good cause to waive Rule 213 where the pleading helped
to ensure a complete and accurate record).

 contains information that the IMM designated as confidential in the IMM Report. The information

 IV.       CONCLUSION

          As the Application demonstrates, the Commission should find that the Transaction is

PUBLIC VERSION

                             UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Grays Harbor Energy LLC                                        )                  Docket No. EC26-76-000
Hardee Power Partners Limited                                  )
Invenergy Cannon Falls LLC                                     )
Invenergy Nelson LLC                                           )
Invenergy Nelson Expansion LLC                                 )
Lackawanna Energy Center LLC                                   )
Spindle Hill Energy LLC                                        )
                                                               )
Gray Wolf Power, LLC                                           )

                               SUPPLEMENTAL AFFIDAVIT OF
                        JULIE R. SOLOMON AND JEFFREY J. OPGRAND

INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

        On March 24, 2026, we filed an affidavit on behalf of the applicants in this docket in
connection with a proposed transaction in which Gray Wolf Power, LLC (“Buyer”) acquires from
InfraBridge North America Thermal Power Acquisition LLC (“InfraBridge” or “Seller”) certain
indirect upstream ownership interests in three existing generating plants located in PJM (the
“Proposed Transaction”). 1

        The purpose of this Supplemental Affidavit is to respond to the Report of the Independent
Market Monitor for PJM (“Report” or “IMM Report”). 2 Nothing in the Report presents any
compelling evidence of an increase in market power as a result of the Proposed Transaction,
particularly in the context of the Commission’s regulations and precedent, and the proposed alleged
“remedies” relate to concerns that are unsupported, discussed in more detail below.

        The IMM Report claims that the Proposed Transaction “would increase market power in the
PJM markets.” 3 In our initial affidavit, as appropriate, we relied on the Commission’s regulations


1
    As part of the Proposed Transaction, Buyer also is acquiring ownership interests in four existing plants outside of
    PJM; such generation is not relevant to this Supplemental Affidavit.
2
    “Market Power Analysis: ArcLight / Invenergy Transaction,” The Independent Market Monitor for PJM, May 26,
    2026 (“IMM Report”).
3
    See IMM Report at 6.


                                                          1
                                               PUBLIC VERSION

applicable in section 203 proceedings to demonstrate that the metrics the Commission typically relies
on to assess market power reflect very modest increases. 4 Indeed, the Delivered Price Test (“DPT”)
results for each relevant market (including PJM, PJM West, AP South, and 5004/5005) identified no
screen failures in generally unconcentrated markets.5 For the capacity market, our initial affidavit
reported an HHI change of 32, based on unforced capacity (“UCAP”) in an unconcentrated market
for the smallest potentially relevant capacity market/LDA (i.e., MAAC). With respect to the PJM-
wide energy market, as well as the capacity market, the IMM agrees with our conclusions, i.e., the
IMM “does not find HHI threshold failures for the aggregate PJM energy and capacity markets or
for submarkets.” 6

        The IMM’s contention that: (i) there will be a material increase in market power in the
aggregate level; (ii) there is an increase in the number of hours in which the Three Pivotal Supplier
(“TPS”) tests are failed in the real-time energy market; and (iii) PJM’s market power mitigation rules
for local market power in the energy market allow suppliers to exercise market power, 7 each have
been previously rejected by the Commission, as discussed below, and should similarly be dismissed
in the instant transaction as well.

        As the Commission concluded with respect to the TPS test in the recent order in Docket
No. EC26-39 [cites excluded]:

        With respect to the PJM IMM’s alternative analyses for the aggregate PJM energy
        market, proposed local energy markets, and the PJM capacity market, including its
        reliance on the three pivotal supplier test, the Commission has previously explained
        that it historically has not relied on three pivotal supplier test results for analysis of
        FPA section 203 transactions and that three pivotal supplier analyses are not
        required from applicants seeking authorization for a proposed transaction under
        FPA section 203. Consistent with this precedent, we will not rely on the PJM

4
    Our analysis is conducted under the assumption that ArcLight will obtain, through the Proposed Transaction, the
    ability to control the energy market offers of all units subject to the Proposed Transaction. However, as described
    in the Application, we understand that ArcLight is not in fact obtaining the governance rights necessary to control
    the day-to-day energy market offers of the units acquired in the Proposed Transaction. As a result, the IMM’s
    hypothetical arguments relating to uneconomic dispatch at any facility acquired in the Proposed Transaction would
    require a third-party entity to choose to pursue such activities.
5
    The Commission no longer considers 5004/5005 as a default relevant submarket within PJM. See KMC Thermo,
    LLC, 195 FERC ¶ 61,082, at P 2 (2026).
6
    See IMM Report at 3.
7
    See IMM Report at 6.


                                                          2
                                                PUBLIC VERSION

         IMM’s three pivotal supplier test results or analysis in this proceeding.
         Accordingly, we reject the PJM IMM’s comments regarding the three pivotal
         supplier test. 8

         Likewise, in that same docket, the Commission rejected the IMM’s request for the
imposition of behavioral mitigation measures, noting that:

         With respect to the PJM IMM’s request that the Commission impose behavioral
         commitments on ArcLight Holdings, we decline to require the requested
         commitments or to otherwise address general issues concerning the PJM markets
         in this proceeding. To challenge a proposed transaction, a party must demonstrate
         that the proposed transaction will have an adverse effect on horizontal competition,
         not that a proposed transaction must have some competitive benefit or market
         enhancement. We find that the PJM IMM has not sufficiently demonstrated that
         the Proposed Transaction would result in any adverse effect on competition to
         support the requested behavioral conditions. As the Commission has previously
         found, arguments based on general concerns about certain elements of PJM’s
         market design that are not specific to a proposed transaction under review are
         beyond the scope of the Commission’s review of the proposed transaction. This
         proceeding, which only concerns the Proposed Transaction, is not the appropriate
         venue for raising or addressing general concerns regarding market design. 9

         Finally, the IMM proposes that the Commission adopt a new relevant submarket in PJM
called “Chesapeake” which “includes but is not limited to the BGE, DOM, and PEPCO
transmission zones.” 10 However, the IMM states that the “Invenergy resources involved in the
Transaction are outside the submarket,” 11 indicating that there is no competitive overlap in the
IMM’s presumed submarket, and a standard “2ab” calculation for the IMM’s “Chesapeake”
submarket would be zero. 12 Hence, setting aside the merits of whether “Chesapeake” constitutes

8
     KMC Thermo, LLC, 195 FERC ¶ 61,082, at P 63 (2026) (footnotes omitted).
9
     KMC Thermo, LLC, 195 FERC ¶ 61,082, at P 65 (2026) (footnotes omitted).
10
     IMM Report page 21. The IMM Report provides links to the PJM website which contain raw data on binding
     constraints and LMPs, but the IMM does not provide any information on dfax used to define Chesapeake.
11
     Comments of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Docket EC26-76, at 10.
12
     The Commission previously has considered HHI changes based on a “2ab” method to be relevant. See, e.g., NRG
     Yield, Inc., 148 FERC ¶ 61,109 at PP 13-14 (2014); AES Corp., 137 FERC ¶ 61,122 at P 24 (2011); SUEZ Energy
     N. Am., Inc., 125 FERC ¶ 61,188 at P 19 (2008); MidAmerican Energy Holdings Co., 113 FERC ¶ 61,298 at P 28
     n.22 (2005), reh’g denied, 118 FERC ¶ 61,003 (2007); Union Elec. Co., 114 FERC ¶ 61,255 (2006). See also N.
     States Power Co. – Minn., 147 FERC ¶ 62,003 at 64,008 & n.3 (2014). The “2ab” method refers to a simplified
     form of the HHI calculation. The market share of company “a” and the market share of company “b” contribute
     a2+b2 to the HHI calculation pre-transaction and (a+b)2 post-transaction. Because (a+b)2 = a2 + b2 + 2ab, subtracting
     the pre-transaction a2+b2 yields 2ab as the calculation of the HHI change.


                                                            3
                                         PUBLIC VERSION

a potentially relevant submarket under Commission precedent, there is no further analysis needed
of the IMM’s proposed “Chesapeake” submarket in the context of this Transaction.

RESPONSE TO THE IMM REPORT

     1.   Energy Market

          The IMM analyzed the impact of the Proposed Transaction on aggregate energy market
concentration using actual generation data and reported that {BEGIN CUI//PRIV} REDACTED
{END CUI//PRIV}. 13 These metrics reflect an increase that is well below the metrics that would
lead the Commission to conclude the presence of a market power concern.

          The IMM analyzes local markets using proprietary TPS test data based on real-time binding
constraints and provides the number of hours for which ArcLight failed the TPS test with and
without the acquisition of the Invenergy assets. The constraints identified were those that bind for
more than five percent of hours during the April 2024 through March 2026 period. The IMM
defines relevant markets based on historical binding transmission constraints in which market
supply “consists of the incremental, effective MW of supply available to relieve the constraint.” 14
To our knowledge, the Commission has not recognized “constraint relief” as a relevant product
market in Section 203 proceedings. Moreover, though the TPS test may provide a measure of the
ability to affect price, it does not address the incentive to attempt to exercise market power.

          The IMM does not provide sufficient information to assess the proposed local “markets”.
Nor does the IMM provide details on the generation resources or locations that are included in the
measure of market supply (including Applicants’ generation), or to what degree the capacity of each
generation resource is adjusted based on distribution factors. Other than the loosely defined
“Chesapeake” market, the IMM does not define the boundaries of the proposed destination market
that delineate the customers affected by the binding transmission constraints in the local market
analysis.

     {BEGIN CUI//PRIV} REDACTED {END CUI//PRIV}



13
     IMM Report Table 5.
14
     IMM Report page 19.


                                                  4
                                              PUBLIC VERSION

         There also are inconsistencies between Table 7 15 and Table 9 16 that are not explained in the
IMM Report. {BEGIN CUI//PRIV} REDACTED {END CUI//PRIV}

     2. Capacity Market

         Table 10 of the IMM Report provides pre- and post- HHIs for ArcLight’s acquisition of the
Invenergy assets for each modeled LDA for the three most recent RPM Base Residual Auctions
(“BRAs”), reporting market concentration for cleared capacity. The results demonstrate no screen
failures based on market concentration and HHI change figures. This is generally consistent with
the analysis presented in our Initial Affidavit, which reported that there were no issues for the PJM-
wide market based on ICAP, and a UCAP analysis of MAAC found an HHI change of 32 points in
an unconcentrated market.

     3. Chesapeake Submarket

         The IMM Report asserts that four frequently binding constraints create the “Chesapeake”
submarket: Bedington-Black Oak, Conastone-Northwest, Graceton-Manor, and Nottingham. 17 Two
of these constraints (Nottingham and Conastone-Northwest) were previously accepted by the
Commission as defining the PJM West submarket. 18 In another matter, the IMM previously
identified the Graceton-Manor constraint as a “Conastone area constraint” that was categorized with
Nottingham and Conastone-Northwest. 19 The IMM Report seems to distinguish “Chesapeake” from
PJM West by (among other things) imposing a “dfax threshold” of three percent to “exclude
resources that do not have a significant impact on a constraint.” 20 In effect, the IMM Report argues
that any resource on the high price side of a constraint with a dfax less than three percent in absolute
value does not qualify as competing supply to deliver to the proposed submarket.


15
     “Constraints where ArcLight had market power as determined by the real-time energy market TPS test: April 2024
     through March 2026 real-time market.”
16
     “Preacquisition and Postacquisition HHI for constraints where ArcLight had market power as determined by the
     real-time energy market TPS test: April 2024 through March 2026.”
17
     See IMM Report at Table 3.
18
     See Darby Power, 192 FERC ¶ 61,073, at 65.
19
     See Market Power Analysis: Constellation Acquisition of Calpine, The Independent Market Monitor for PJM, March
     25, 2025, at Table 1.
20
     IMM Report at 24.


                                                         5
                                              PUBLIC VERSION

          In our Initial Affidavit, we performed a DPT for the PJM West submarket and found no
screen failures, with HHI changes ranging from 5-17 points in an unconcentrated market. Further,
ArcLight controls a de minimis share of generation in the IMM’s proposed “Chesapeake” submarket,
and the transaction does not alter that share because the “Invenergy resources involved in the
Transaction are outside the submarket.” 21,22

          The IMM Report articulates a strategy involving “Local Market Power on Both Sides of the
Constraint”. 23 The discussion is intended to “demonstrate that a self scheduled or a low offer
generation on the lower price side of a transmission constraint could increase the prices on the higher
price side of the transmission constraint.” 24 The IMM Report presents a stylized example of how a
generating unit could self-schedule itself on the low-price side of a constraint in order to increase
flows on a transmission line and create a binding constraint, thus causing price separation. As we
have noted, the IMM acknowledges that Lackawanna is not located in the “Chesapeake” submarket,
hence it is on the low-price side of the purported Chesapeake constraints.

          By adding Lackawanna to its portfolio, ArcLight would have less of an incentive to engage
in the IMM’s purported uneconomic overproduction on the low-price side of the “Chesapeake”
constraints, for the following reason. ArcLight currently controls generation on both sides of the
purported “Chesapeake” constraints; with the acquisition of Lackawanna, it will control an increased
amount of generation that would suffer from the price-depressing effect of such a strategy on the
low-price side. ArcLight is not acquiring any generation within “Chesapeake” that would benefit
from such a strategy. Hence, the Proposed Transaction is not anti-competitive with respect to the
IMM’s purported “low offer generation on the lower price side of a transmission constraint” strategy.

          The IMM Report presents no empirical evidence that ArcLight, as a result of the Proposed
Transaction, will have the incentive to exercise “Local Market Power on Both Sides of the
Constraint.” The discussion is theoretical and mischaracterizes ArcLight’s incentives. Indeed,



21
     Comments of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Docket EC26-76, at 10.
22
     Based on PJM’s 27/28 Reliability Pricing Model, there is 34,583 MWs of installed capacity in the BGE, DOM, and
     PEPCO zones combined. ArcLight controls only 996 MWs in those zones, or 2.9%.
23
     IMM Report at 32-35.
24
     Id., at 34.


                                                         6
                                              PUBLIC VERSION

ArcLight will control substantially more generation outside of “Chesapeake” than inside of it. 25 Nor
does the IMM Report present evidence that ArcLight (or any market participant) engages in such a
strategy today, even though ArcLight currently controls generation on both sides of the identified
constraints (and several market participants do as well). The claim that {BEGIN CUI//PRIV}
REDACTED {END CUI//PRIV} is entirely unsupported. And finally, even in the unlikely
instances in which the data (on a backward-looking basis) appear to suggest that a market participant
would have the incentive and ability to profitably attempt such a strategy, executing the strategy in
real-time is much more complicated. Market participants do not know in advance which constraints
will be binding in future time intervals, what their competitors’ generation offers will be, the
distribution and magnitude of load in future price intervals, etc. By attempting such a strategy,
uneconomical overproduction at a generation facility is almost guaranteed to decrease profits, and
the potential gains from increasing prices on the opposite side of a predicted constraint are risky at
best.

         For the reasons discussed in this section, we conclude that the Proposed Transaction does not
raise horizontal market power concerns with respect to the IMM Report’s “Local Market Power on
Both Sides of the Constraint” analysis, and there are no market power concerns with respect to the
IMM Report’s supposed “Chesapeake” submarket.

CONCLUSION

         The energy and capacity market analyses submitted with the Application clearly support the
conclusion that the Proposed Transaction will not have adverse competitive effects in any relevant
market. There is no significant increase in any of the metrics the Commission consistently applies
in the evaluation of such transactions.




25
     Based on PJM’s 27/28 Reliability Pricing Model, ArcLight controls 8,140 MWs, and the Transaction will add
     another 2,327 MWs, for a total of 10,471 MWs outside of “Chesapeake”. This is more than ten times the amount of
     capacity that ArcLight controls inside of “Chesapeake” (996 MW). As a result, it is highly unlikely that an
     uneconomic increase in generation affecting the prices realized outside of “Chesapeak,” where ArcLight controls
     more than 10 times the amount of generation inside of “Chesapeake,” would produce an economic gain on a
     consolidated basis.


                                                         7
                                       PUBLIC VERSION

correct.


Executed the 10th day of June 2026.



Julie R. Solomon

Jeffrey J. Opgrand
